Introduction - January 2012

#### **Introduction** **•****_The New Year has started with mixed_** **_sentiment. The problems besetting the Eurozone are being partially offset by hopes for renewed growth and this latter has underpinned the early improvement in commodity prices. It may well be too soon for this optimism to pay off and we expect to see metals prices struggle to make much more headway in the first few weeks of the year. The longer-term outlook is brighter._** **•****_Gold has started 2012 on a more positive_** **_note than in the fourth quarter of 2011 with physical demand strengthening and some investors re-establishing long positions. We expect gold to make new highs in the latter part of 2012 as investors hedge against fiat currency risk and anticipate inflationary pressures. In the near term, however, the market is still cautious. When the Chinese New Year and Indian wedding seasons are over a slip in physical demand may combine with this nervousness to undermine prices again in February._** **•****_Silver remains unsettled. Its renewed_** **_propensity for very sharp falls during 2011, combined with its poor fundamental balance are deterring investors who, if they are looking to hedge against risk are more likely to prefer gold. That said, a strong run in gold later in the year would pull silver with it, but we see silver continuing to struggle in the near term._** ##### **~~Precious Metals Medium Term Relative Performance~~** 340

**I1** Economic Indicators - January 2012 ##### **Interest rates; varied enough to encourage gold investment** At the start of January the benchmark interest rates in a number of major countries are close to zero. The Federal Reserve policy rate is 0-0.25%, while that of the Bank of Japan is 0-0.1%; the European Central Bank rate is 1.0% but is widely expected to be cut in the next few weeks; the Swiss National Bank is at 0.25% and at the Bank of England the rate is 0.5%. Meanwhile in the fact of sustained turmoil in the Eurozone, Italian ten-year bond yields are just below the “danger level” of 7% (this is the yield at which is becomes almost impossible to refinance existing debt), while Spanish bond yields are between 5.0% and 5.5%. The Greek two-year yield, meanwhile, is at a massive 138%. Spanish and Italian yields have in fact been coming down slightly in the secondary markets in early January and this has had an indirect impact on the metals markets. These are government rates and are therefore arguably misleading in that they do not necessarily reflect daily market movements. US Treasury notes are more telling in this regard; the current yield on US 2-year notes stands at below 0.3%, while the yield on 3-month US Treasury Bills is just 0.015%. Part of the reason for improved metals prices at the start of this year is, arguably, that there is a glimmer of optimism over the prospects for the Eurozone’s economic growth. The purchasing in these high-yielding bond markets has come from long-term investors ascribing to this view and who have thus been looking to lock in yield. A bounce ensued and after closing 2011 at $1,547.50, gold had regained $1,637 by 10th January. Gold registered an intra-year gain of 10.3% during 2011, making it the best performer among the precious metals, and indeed outpacing the major base metals also. Sentiment towards gold had soured to a degree among some investors during the final weeks of 2011, as the dollar took an increasingly important role as the safe haven of choice. Gold’s sharp fall in September had been driven not only by investors’ flight from risk, which affected the commodities as a whole, but was exacerbated by liquidation in order to raise cash against potential margin calls elsewhere. Gold’s subsequent failure to regain the old September highs meant that some would-be interest in the metal was lost. Further, there were some participants in the financial markets who were concerned that an escalation of problems in the European banking sector would result in more gold liquidation. Gold lending and selling thus proved to be a key for some institutions to gain access to dollars. ##### **Risk aversion; bearish for gold in the short term, but bullish for much of 2012** These factors meant that during December, gold was again vulnerable, especially in mid-month when the commodities were again under particular pressure due to fresh fears over the Eurozone crisis in the wake of a Summit that was widely seen as disappointing. In this particularly sharp fall, gold dropped from just over $1,710 to just below $1,575 (intraday prices) from the 12th-14th December inclusive. Sales were amplified by market participants looking to move into the money markets in an effort to minimise risk and reduce volatility, while also wanting to increase their dollar holdings. In mid-December there was very heavy dollar borrowing from the European Central Bank in the face of sclerosis in the European banking sector, with banks borrowing $51Bn of three months dollar instruments in one auction. This surge in borrowing followed the action by six major central banks to reduce the cost to European banks of borrowing dollars via the dollar swap process in an effort to improve liquidity in the European system (swap prices did remain relatively high, however, in the face of strong demand). There are also other elements to consider. The financial position at the start of 2012 resembles that of 2009, in the wake of the Lehman Brothers crash of September 2008, with liquidity pumped into the markets and risk aversion remaining high. In early January gold is starting to regain support in the professional market as well as in the physical sector, but the falls of the final quarter of 2011 suggest that parts of the market will remain cautious and the market needs some time to consolidate. While allowing for the possibility of bouts of distressed sales in the event of more problems in the Eurozone, it is likely that most weak-handed holders are now out of the market and that the first quarter of this year will lay the foundations for renewed gains over the rest of 2012 as investors hedge medium-term inflationary and currency-related fears. We are looking for the price to challenge $2,000 before 2012 is out. Our time frame for this has now been pushed back towards the end of this year following the market’s weak performance in December, but the argument for renewed strength in price remains unaltered. The pattern of the market’s fundamentals plus the economic and financial backdrop suggest that the long-term bull market is approaching maturity and we would expect investment activity to start to wane during 2013. ##### **Activity in the gold markets** Activity in the Chinese gold market, as measured by the turnover on the Shanghai Gold Exchange, soared at the end of December and remained high into the first week of January. Average daily November turnover on the SGE was 6.5 tonnes, rising to almost eleven tonnes when prices dipped. In December, by contrast, the daily average in the first fortnight, before the price started its heavy slide, was 7.2 tonnes; over the rest of the month the daily average was 12.5 tonnes and the first few days of January averaged 14.9 tonnes per day. Furthermore the average premium over loco London prices jumped higher as international prices dropped. In the first half of the month the premium averaged 0.05% and for half of that time the SGE price was actually at a discount to the international market.
